1.rendering: Hebrew YHWH rendered as 'the Eternal' in third person and 'Eternal' in direct address — the Aperto EN project-wide divine-name canonicalisation. The vocative anchor of the psalm: addressed to this specific name from first word to last.
1.tradeOff: Traded the familiarity of 'the LORD' (the standard English convention) for a name that reads as a name rather than a title. The cost is unfamiliarity to readers raised on KJV-tradition English; the gain is that the I–Thou address of the psalm — a person being addressed by name from word one to word last — survives the translation.

1.rendering: Hebrew ḥāqar rendered 'search' at both ends of the psalm: v. 1 'you have searched me' (indicative) and v. 23 'Search me' (imperative). Only the mood changes; the verb stays identical so the inclusio is audible. Not 'examine,' not 'scan,' not 'know fully.'
1.tradeOff: Traded lexical variation for frame integrity. 'Examine' or 'scan' would each render the line plausibly, but the reader must hear the end answer the beginning — the same verb returning in a different mood is the whole theological move of the psalm.

1.rendering: Hebrew yādaʿ held to one English verb — 'know' — across all seven occurrences (vv. 1, 2, 4, 6 as the noun daʿat, 14, 23×2). No variation to 'perceive,' 'discern,' 'be aware,' or 'recognise' for elegance, since those render other Hebrew verbs (bîn, zārâ, sākan) the psalm keeps distinct. v. 1: 'known me.'
1.tradeOff: Traded English literary variation — the impulse to swap synonyms across a long poem — for the keyword integrity that is the psalm's main structural device. A reader who only ever meets 'know' across 24 verses cannot miss that this is the psalm's central verb.

16.tradeOff: Traded the biological precision the proof-text tradition wants ('embryo' is the gloss anti-abortion campaigning needs) for the psalm's actual semantic range. The cost: less rhetorically useful in a particular political fight; the gain: the line means what the word means, and the Jewish golem afterlife (impossible if collapsed to 'embryo') is preserved.

16.rendering: Hebrew sēfer rendered 'your scroll' — the heavenly record on which days are inscribed. Carried by the KULTUR footnote that names what the image is NOT (cold predestination) and what it IS (being kept in mind, attended to, held by name before the days are lived).
16.tradeOff: Traded the modernised 'your book' for the more accurate 'your scroll,' which keeps the ancient-Near-Eastern register and prevents the line from reading as a Reformation-era proof-text for predestination. The cost: 'scroll' is slightly archaic; the gain: the image stays itself.

16.rendering: v. 16c follows the ketiv reading: 'the days that were shaped for me — before the first of them began.' Keeps the genuinely hard Hebrew syntax (lit. 'and not one of them was'): God's seeing precedes any finished shape, even the shape of the days themselves. The verse stays uncomfortable; it is meant to.
16.tradeOff: Traded the smoother qere reading (which yields a tidier 'when as yet there were none of them') for the harder ketiv the exegesis §A.4 prefers. The reader has to slow down; that is the point.

16.rendering: All 24 verses always presented together. v. 16 specifically refused as a 'God-knows-your-days' devotional clip detached from the harder syntax.
16.tradeOff: Traded the easier devotional reception for textual honesty.

16.rendering: I–Thou throughout. v. 16 is a Thou seeing — not an abstract claim about foreknowledge.

17.rendering: Hebrew yāqar rendered 'weighty' — 'How weighty to me are your thoughts, my God.' Resolves the genuine translator fork (precious vs. weighty) toward weighty. The parallel colon 'how vast is the sum' (v. 17b) leans to weight; Goldingay reads 'weighty/formidable.' Carries gravity, not preciousness. The German edition chose the weighty reading; EN follows for consistency.
17.tradeOff: Traded the NIV-familiar 'precious' for a word that carries awe rather than sentiment. 'Precious' is the safer, sweeter choice and the more emotionally accessible English; 'weighty' is colder and risks sounding clinical, but matches the psalm's gravity register and the parallel colon's vastness imagery.

17.rendering: Hebrew rēaʿ rendered 'thoughts' — 'your thoughts.' Echoes 'my thoughts' at v. 2: speaker's intentions known by God; God's thoughts marvelled at by speaker. The cross-reference is deliberate.

19.rendering: Hebrew ʾĕlôah — the rare Job-name for God — rendered 'O God' in the line, with a HARM footnote at v. 19 carrying the Job-signal (the wisdom/innocent-sufferer kinship). English has no distinct poetic God-word to carry the rare register, so the line takes the available vocative and the footnote does the scholarship.
19.tradeOff: Traded lexical distinction in the line for footnote-carried scholarship. Three different Hebrew divine names appear in this psalm; English has fewer registers to deploy. The compromise: differentiate where English permits (the Eternal / my God), let the footnote do the work where it doesn't.

19.rendering: Hebrew ʾim-tiqṭōl rendered 'If only you would kill the wicked, O God' — an optative, a wish handed wholly to God. NEVER an imperative ('Kill the wicked!') and NEVER a hypothetical conditional. The grammar is the ethics: the psalmist commands nothing, asks no human to act.
19.tradeOff: Traded the punchier imperative (which the rage of the line invites) for the grammatically correct optative. The cost: 'If only you would' is slightly softer in English mouth-feel; the gain: the psalm's central ethical claim — violence is given to God, not enacted by the speaker — survives.

19.rendering: Hebrew qāṭal rendered 'kill' — blunt and modern. NOT 'slay' (archaic in contemporary English, carries the KJV register Aperto avoids). The Hebrew verb is blunt; the English should be blunt.
19.tradeOff: Traded the older devotional register ('slay' has biblical-poetic resonance for many readers) for contemporary plainness. The cost: 'kill' lands harder, can feel shocking in a psalm; the gain: that shock IS the psalm, not a translation overreach.

19.rendering: v. 19b addressed to the killers (NOT to God): 'you who thirst for blood — turn away from me.' Distinct addressee from the wish in 19a. The line is dismissal of the violent, not petition to the deity.
19.tradeOff: Traded the smoother continuous-address reading (everything in v. 19 to God) for the shift in addressee the Hebrew syntax requires. The cost: a sharper mid-verse turn the reader must catch; the gain: the speaker's actual ethical posture — handing rage to God, telling killers to leave — is preserved.

19.rendering: Stanza 4 (vv. 19–24) takes EN-P3 hardness — fragmentary, harder syntax, sharper register — even though the governing style code for the whole psalm is EN-P2 (intimate trust). The blank-line break (\b) before v. 19 is the sharpest turn in the psalm and is NOT softened, NOT bridged.
19.tradeOff: Traded register uniformity (one style for the whole poem) for register accuracy (one poem with a turn). The cost: the translator and reader both have to handle two registers across a single text; the gain: the psalm's actual shape — wonder, then sudden hardness, then quiet petition — survives the translation.

19.rendering: All 24 verses always presented together. v. 19 specifically refused as the excisable verse the Revised Common Lectionary cuts — the HARM footnote at v. 19 names this directly.
19.tradeOff: Traded the easier liturgical reception for textual honesty. The rage is named in full and then handed over; cutting it rewrites the psalm.

22.rendering: Hebrew taklît śinʾâ rendered 'complete hatred' — taklît names totality / completeness / the full extent of a thing. NEVER 'perfect hatred' (KJV — implies morally flawless, virtuous hate; documented harm history at §C.5 #3). The UEBERSETZUNG footnote at v. 22 names the harm history explicitly: 'perfect hatred' has been used to license righteous-feeling contempt for enemies that the optative grammar of v. 19 refuses.
22.tradeOff: Traded the rhetorical heft of the KJV phrase (which still echoes in many readers' ears as a beloved devotional line) for an English that means what the Hebrew means. 'Complete' is plainer than 'perfect'; that is the point — the hatred is total, not virtuous.

23.rendering: Hebrew ḥāqar rendered 'Search me' (imperative) — answering v. 1's 'you have searched me' (indicative). The inclusio closes: the one who was searched without consent now asks to be. Only mood changed; verb identical.
23.tradeOff: Traded lexical variation for frame integrity. The reader must hear the end answer the beginning — the same verb returning in a different mood is the whole theological move of the psalm.

23.tradeOff: Traded variation for keyword integrity. 'Know my heart… discern my thoughts' would smooth the line but break the count.

24.rendering: Hebrew derek ʿôlām rendered 'the everlasting way' — resolving the translator fork toward §F.9's preferred reading. The contrast with v. 24a's derek-ʿōṣeb ('hurtful way') is kept: two 'ways.' The LEBEN footnote at v. 24 flags the dual sense of ʿôlām (everlasting / ancient — cf. Jer 6:16) and opens onto the contemplative-examen tradition ('Search me. Know my heart. Lead me.').
24.tradeOff: Traded the equally defensible 'ancient way' (which has its own scriptural resonance via Jeremiah 6:16) for 'everlasting way.' Both senses live in ʿôlām; the line takes one, the footnote keeps both.

24.rendering: Stanza 4 (vv. 19–24) takes EN-P3 hardness — but the closing line of v. 24 lands the softest of the stanza: 'lead me in the everlasting way.' The hardness has passed; what remains is the asking. The LEBEN footnote names the verb-echo with v. 10 ('your hand would lead me') — same verb, menace gone, gentle now.
24.tradeOff: Traded register uniformity (which would keep v. 24 as hard as v. 22) for the closing shift the Hebrew makes. The cost: a register modulation inside a single stanza; the gain: the poem lands open-handed, as the exegesis says.

24.rendering: All 24 verses always presented together. v. 24 is the final word — being led, not vindicated — and depends on every preceding verse to mean what it means.
24.tradeOff: Traded the easier liturgical reception for textual honesty.

24.rendering: I–Thou throughout. v. 24's 'lead me' is the relational close — the speaker handing themselves to a Thou who leads, not invoking an attribute.

24.rendering: Governing style code EN-P2 (Intimate Trust) — and v. 24's closing petition is the verse the whole code is built for: quiet, first-person, present-tense, understated. The poem ends where its register lives.
